title: Find Longest Self-Contained Substring
statement:
Given a string `s`, a substring `t` of `s` is **self-contained** when two things hold:

- `t` is not the whole of `s`, and
- every letter that occurs in `t` has all of its occurrences in `s` inside `t`; no copy of it appears in the part of `s` outside `t`.

Return the length of the longest self-contained substring of `s`, or `-1` if `s` has none.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Checking every substring against the letter counts is O(26 · n²). A shortcut comes from the first character of a self-contained substring: all copies of that letter must be inside, so the substring has to **start at the first occurrence** of its first letter. There are at most 26 such starting points. From each one, scan right: any letter whose first occurrence lies before `start` makes every longer substring from `start` invalid, and every letter seen forces the substring to stretch at least to that letter's last occurrence. Whenever the scan reaches the farthest required position, the substring is closed and self-contained.

## Approach

1. Record `first` and `last`, the first and last index of each letter.
2. For each `start` in `first`'s values (one per distinct letter), set `end = start`.
3. Scan `i` from `start`. If `s[i]` first appears before `start`, stop: no longer substring from here can work.
4. Otherwise stretch `end` to `last` of `s[i]`.
5. When `i === end`, `s[start..end]` holds every copy of every letter in it. If it is shorter than `s`, update `best`.
6. Return `best`, which stays `-1` when nothing qualifies.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abba"`: `first = {a: 0, b: 1}`, `last = {a: 3, b: 2}`.

- `start = 0`: `a` stretches `end` to 3, and `i` reaches 3 with `end = 3`, but length 4 is the whole string, so it is skipped.
- `start = 1`: `b` stretches `end` to 2; at `i = 2`, `i === end`, length 2, so `best = 2`. At `i = 3`, `a` first appears at 0 < 1, so the scan stops.

The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(26 · n): at most 26 starts, each scanning the string once.
- Space: O(26): two maps keyed by letter.

## Pitfalls

- The whole string never counts, even though it trivially contains all its letters.
- Stopping only when `i === end` matters: an earlier `i` still has letters whose later copies lie outside.
- A start that is not a first occurrence can never work, which is why only 26 starts are needed.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `first`, `last` | first and last index of each letter |
| `start` | where the candidate substring begins |
| `end` | farthest index the candidate must reach |
| `i` | current scan position |
| `best` | longest self-contained length so far, or -1 |

narration.3: first maps each letter to the index where it first appears.
narration.4: last maps each letter to the index where it last appears.
narration.5: One pass over the string fills both maps.
narration.7: Only the first sighting of a letter is stored in first.
narration.9: Every sighting overwrites last, so it ends at the final one.
narration.13: A valid substring must begin at some letter's first occurrence, so try only those starts.
narration.14: So far the substring only needs to reach start itself.
narration.15: Extend the candidate one character at a time.
narration.16: This letter also occurs before start, so no substring from start can include it.
narration.19: Every copy of this letter must be included, so stretch end to its last occurrence.
narration.20: Reached the farthest required index, and the substring is not the whole string.
narration.21: It is self-contained; keep its length if it is the longest.
narration.25: Return the longest length found, or -1.
